title: Walter Scott's Letters on Demonology: Popular Historicization of Witch Trials
description: Walter Scott published Letters on Demonology and Witchcraft in 1830 as part of the 'Family Library' series, producing the first widely read popular historical account of witch trials aimed at a general readership. Scott drew on earlier antiquarian and scholarly work to present witchcraft prosecution as a historical phenomenon belonging to a past age of superstition — firmly located in history and safely distant from the present. The book went through multiple editions and shaped Victorian popular understanding of witch trials as products of mass hysteria and ignorance. Scott's framing — witch persecution as the result of superstition and credulity rather than rational process — became the dominant popular narrative for over a century.
historiographical_note: Scott's rationalist-superstition framework was challenged by all major twentieth-century historians. Keith Thomas, Alan Macfarlane, and especially Stuart Clark rejected the idea that witch persecutors were simply irrational, arguing instead that witch belief was rational within its own framework. Scott's narrative persisted in popular culture long after historians had abandoned it, illustrating the gap between academic and popular historiography.
source_method: Scott, Letters on Demonology and Witchcraft (1830); secondary scholarship on the historiography of witchcraft
